t: Friends are generally united by a belief in each human's ability to be guided by the inward light, and they avoid creeds and hierarchical structures to differing extents.

Early Quakers were persecuted in England and in Massachusetts, where four were executed, and the Quaker Act 1662 and the Conventicle Act 1664 were used against them, until the Act of Toleration of 1689.

Quakers refused oaths and war and opposed slavery; nine of the twelve founders of the Society for the Abolition of the Slave Trade were Quakers, and Quaker service bodies shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947.
dyk: The name Quaker began as ridicule: according to George Fox's autobiography, the magistrate Gervase Bennet was the first to call them Quakers, because Fox told him to tremble at the word of the Lord.
ev: George Fox has a vision on Pendle Hill in Lancashire in which he believes the Lord shows him where a great people is to be gathered
The English Quaker missionaries Mary Fisher and Ann Austin begin preaching in Boston and are imprisoned for five weeks and banished
Mary Dyer is hanged near Boston Common for repeatedly defying a law banning Quakers from the colony
William Penn establishes Pennsylvania as a commonwealth run under Quaker principles, after founding West Jersey in 1676
The Act of Toleration ends the official persecution of dissenters in England
The first petition against the slave trade is presented to Parliament by a group of six Quakers
The Great Separation divides American Friends into Hicksite and Orthodox yearly meetings
The British Friends Service Council and the American Friends Service Committee are awarded the Nobel Peace Prize

f.where: England and Wales, Ireland, the Netherlands, Barbados and the American colonies from the 17th century; today chiefly Africa (49% of adult Friends in 2017) and North America (22%), with Kenya, the United States, Burundi and Bolivia holding the most
f.period: arose in mid-17th-century England; persecuted until the Act of Toleration 1689; Quietist period in the 18th century; splits in the 19th century; Quaker Renaissance from the late 19th century; worldwide and still active
f.figures: George Fox, the founder; Margaret Fell, who with Fox developed new conceptions of family and community; Robert Barclay, divine; William Penn, founder of Pennsylvania; Mary Dyer, hanged in Boston in 1660; Elias Hicks, Joseph John Gurney and John Wilbur, around whom nineteenth-century branches formed; Rufus Jones and John Wilhelm Rowntree of the Quaker Renaissance
f.outcome: persecution in England ended after 1689; the numbers fell in the 18th and 19th centuries and the Society divided into branches; Friends became known for opposition to slavery and war, for business and schools, and for relief work, sharing the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947
